Type specialization is layered on top: matmul_static_bf16.cc, matmul_static_sfp.cc, matmul_static_i8.cc, matmul_static_nuq.cc, and matmul_static_f32.cc each compile the full kernel set for one weight type, with MatMulStatic, L29 as the generated overload per ISA target.

Numerics are treated with unusual care for a hobbyist-scale project. The ConditionNumber, L51 helper in the dot product code estimates how many mantissa bits a given weight/vector pair actually needs, and error-compensated cascaded sums keep accumulation accurate. This is a nice reminder that inference quality on compressed weights is not luck — it is measured, Dot, L421 by Dot, L414.

From Install to Your First Model

The build is plain CMake with FetchContent pulling four dependencies: Highway, SentencePiece, nlohmann/json, and cpp-httplib. On Unix:

git clone https://github.com/google/gemma.cpp.git
cd gemma.cpp
cmake --preset make
cmake --build --preset make -j8

On Windows, use cmake --preset windows instead (the README recommends WSL or the Visual Studio Build Tools with the Clang toolset). Bazel users can bazel build -c opt --cxxopt=-std=c++20 :gemma.

Weights come from Kaggle: pick the “Gemma C++” variation of gemma-2, consent to the license, download, and extract with tar -xf archive.tar.gz. Start with gemma2-2b-it-sfp — the 8-bit switching-float variant is half the size of BF16 and faster to run. Then:

./gemma --tokenizer tokenizer.spm --weights gemma2-2b-it-sfp.sbs

(Models in the newer single-file format embed the tokenizer, so you can drop the --tokenizer flag entirely; io/migrate_weights converts older checkpoints.)

To embed the engine rather than chat with it, the pattern fits in one screen — this is a condensed version of the repo’s examples/hello_world/run.cc:

#include "gemma/gemma.h"
#include "gemma/gemma_args.h"
#include "util/threading_context.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  gcpp::LoaderArgs loader(argc, argv);      // --weights, --tokenizer
  gcpp::InferenceArgs inference(argc, argv);
  gcpp::ThreadingContext ctx;               // thread pools, caches
  gcpp::MatMulEnv env(ctx);                 // autotuning + scratch
  gcpp::Gemma gemma(loader, inference, ctx);
  gcpp::KVCache kv_cache(gemma.Config(), inference, ctx.allocator);

  const std::vector<int> tokens = gcpp::WrapAndTokenize(
      gemma.Tokenizer(), gemma.ChatTemplate(),
      gemma.Config().wrapping, 0, "Write a greeting to the world.");

  gcpp::RuntimeConfig rc = {
      .max_generated_tokens = 1024,
      .temperature = 1.0,
      .verbosity = 0,
      .stream_token = [](int token, float) { /* print */ return true; },
  };
  gcpp::TimingInfo timing;
  gemma.Generate(rc, tokens, 0, kv_cache, env, timing);
}

Five objects, one call. For comparison, standing up a full TGI container to serve the same model involves considerably more moving parts — which is precisely the trade gemma.cpp is making in reverse.

Honest Limits

Credit where due: the README does not oversell, and neither should we. Here is what this engine genuinely is not.

  • CPU only. There is no CUDA, Metal, or Vulkan path. Everything runs through Highway’s CPU SIMD. If you need GPU throughput, look elsewhere; this is a research and embedding tool, not a throughput machine.
  • A gated, narrow model menu. Weights must be downloaded through Kaggle’s consent flow, and conversion from other sources is only partially public — the safetensors converter is described as “not yet open sourced.” The supported set is Gemma 2, Gemma 3, and PaliGemma 2; fine-tunes require converting to .sbs yourself.
  • The “tiny” label is load-bearing but selective. The 2K-LoC claim covers the model core; add the matmul/autotuning layer, the compression library, IO, and threading utilities and the real surface is closer to 6K lines — plus whatever you need to learn about Highway. Simplicity here means “one flat repo,” not “naive code.”
  • Experimental edges. CLI usage is flagged experimental in the docs, long sequences get quadratic-attention slow, and while an SSE-style HTTP server binary now ships alongside the CLI, this is not a hardened multi-tenant serving stack. Treat it as the readable reference implementation that production systems — and other tutorials — can be checked against.

Those limits are also the point. gemma.cpp is one of the few places where you can read an entire inference engine — weights on disk, decompression, tiling, autotuning, sampling — without a guided tour. This post was that tour; the diff to your own fork is the next step.
entry.summary: A source tour of gemma.cpp: how its .sbs weight format, SIMD matmul kernels, tokenizer, and top-k sampling fit into a ~2K LoC C++ transformer engine.

entry.title: MaxText: Inside Google’s JAX Blueprint for TPU-Scale LLM Training and Serving

link.title: MaxText: Inside Google’s JAX Blueprint for TPU-Scale LLM Training and Serving

entry.content:
Most LLM frameworks you meet on this blog start from PyTorch and bend toward accelerators. MaxText starts from the opposite shore: it is a pure Python / JAX reference implementation built first for Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs, and it treats the compiler — XLA — as the place where performance comes from. There is no hand-written CUDA everywhere, no bespoke scheduler; instead there is a very carefully organized set of model definitions, a declarative sharding layer, and a training loop that trusts jax.jit to fuse everything. If gemma-cpp showed us what it takes to squeeze a Gemma-class model into a laptop CPU, MaxText is the other pole: the same family of models expressed so they can scale to tens of thousands of chips.

The project recently went through a structural reorganization (tracked in its RESTRUCTURE.md), so the layout we tour today is the modern one: the Python package lives under src/maxtext/, with subfolders like models/, layers/, trainers/pre_train/, common/, utils/, and inference/. Old tutorials that reference a top-level MaxText/ directory are now stale; the module you import is maxtext, and entry points are python3 -m maxtext.trainers.pre_train.train for training and python3 -m maxtext.inference.decode for sampling. Keeping that map in your head makes the rest of the tour much easier.

What makes MaxText worth a source tour is how few moving parts it needs to hit state-of-the-art model FLOPs utilization. Configs are YAML files. Sharding is described with logical axis names that get resolved against a physical device mesh. The training step is one function. Checkpointing delegates to Orbax. Serving is an engine class with four verbs — load_params, prefill, insert, generate — that JetStream-style servers call. Let’s walk through the whole flow with two diagrams.

The overview graph: pyconfig builds HyperParameters, the training loop wraps a jitted train_step, logical sharding resolves against a physical device mesh, the Transformer decomposes into decoder/attention/MLP layers, and MaxEngine serves decode on the same model.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • pyconfig.initialize, L415 — loads base.yml, a model YAML, then CLI/env overrides, and hands back a validated HyperParameters object.
  • create_device_mesh, L2028 — turns ici_parallelism / dcn_parallelism numbers into a concrete jax.Mesh over your devices.
  • create_sharding, L489 — resolves logical names like activation_batch and embed into a NamedSharding on that mesh.
  • train_step, L499 — the jitted heart of pre-training: value-and-grad over loss_fn, gradient casting, optimizer update.
  • Transformer, L108 — a Flax NNX module wiring an Embed table to an NNXDecoder stack.
  • NNXDecoder, L549 — scans layers in a loop or splits them across mesh stages for staged data flow.
  • Attention, L93 — QKV projection, RoPE, and a dispatch table of fused kernels.
  • MaxEngine, L110 — the serving engine: load_params, prefill, insert, generate.
  • main, L89 — the CLI decode loop that exercises all of the above in one process.

The Config Machine

Everything in MaxText begins with pyconfig. The function pyconfig.initialize, L415 is a thin wrapper around _initialize_pydantic, which does something subtly clever: it loads src/maxtext/configs/base.yml (about a thousand keys of documented defaults), then merges a config path — either passed explicitly or inferred from model_name — and finally applies CLI overrides via OmegaConf. When you type model_name=llama3-8b, MaxText finds src/maxtext/configs/models/llama3-8b.yml, which itself inherits from base.yml, and layers the deltas on top.

Validation happens through a Pydantic schema: MaxTextConfig, L4189 in configs/types.py declares every knob with a type, a default, and (often) a comment about units. The runtime object, HyperParameters at L333, wraps that Pydantic model and forwards attribute access, so config.per_device_batch_size just works. This design has a pleasant property: the same code path serves training, compilation, and inference, and every one of them sees an identical, already-validated view of the world. The cost is sprawl — base.yml is enormous, and a surprising fraction of onboarding is learning which of the hundred-plus keys actually matter for your run.

Sharding: Physical Meshes, Logical Names

MaxText’s sharding story is the part most worth stealing for your own JAX projects. The entry point is create_device_mesh, L2028: given ici_parallelism (how axes split inside a TPU slice) and dcn_parallelism (how slices split across the data center network), it builds a physical mesh, filling in any unspecified axes automatically. Multi-slice runs get a hybrid mesh; single slices can opt into split physical axes with allow_split_physical_axes.

On top of that physical mesh sits a logical vocabulary. Layers never write PartitionSpec("data", "tensor"); they write names like activation_batch, activation_norm_length, activation_embed, activation_mlp. The resolver logical_to_mesh_axes, L452 maps those logical names through logical_axis_rules to real mesh axes, and create_sharding, L489 returns a ready-to-use NamedSharding. Because the mapping is data, you can re-target a model from an 8-chip host to a 3-dimensional megascale cluster by editing rules rather than touching layer code. It is the same philosophical bet as ZeRO-style state sharding in deepspeed — push partitioning decisions into a declarative layer — but expressed natively in JAX’s sharding semantics rather than as a PyTorch plugin.

Inside the Training Step

The training entry point trainers/pre_train/train.py is refreshingly linear: main parses argv, initialize builds the config, and train_loop at L1192 calls setup_train_loop, L358 to assemble the mesh, optimizer, sharded state, checkpoint manager, and the jitted step function via jit_train_step, L235. State lives in TrainStateNNX, L26, which unifies the Flax NNX model state and the Optax optimizer state in one module so a single jit boundary captures everything.

The step itself, train_step, L499, splits the NNX model into params and rest, computes jax.value_and_grad over loss_fn, L133 — a shared forward used by both train and eval — casts gradients to grad_dtype, applies gradient accumulation over microbatches when configured, and hands the result to the optimizer. MoE models get extra machinery: router-bias updates, overflow rollback, and auxiliary load-balancing losses threaded through the same function.

Durability is a first-class concern at ten-thousand-chip scale, and it shows. save_checkpoint, L1565 wraps Orbax’s async CheckpointManager — created earlier by create_orbax_checkpoint_manager — blocking only when metrics require it, saving in a layout that keeps NNX and legacy Linen checkpoints interchangeable. On restore, load_state_if_possible, L730 implements the priority chain you can read at the top of base.yml: resume the latest full checkpoint if one exists, else load_parameters_path, else load_full_state_path, else initialize fresh. Preemption is expected, not exceptional.

Serving: Prefill, Insert, Generate

Serving reuses the exact same model code through a different facade. MaxEngine in inference/maxengine/maxengine.py creates its own device mesh at L121, loads or converts params, and exposes the JetStream-compatible verb set. A request flows through three phases: prefill, L774 runs the prompt through the model in one shot and returns the first token plus a populated cache; insert, L1505 places that result into a decode slot; then generate, L1136 steps the whole batch one token per call, with the heavy function jitted and the cache donated in place.

The KV cache itself is worth a look: KVCache, L153 manages paged, layer-stacked arrays with configurable axis orders for prefill versus autoregressive mode, plus quantization hooks for the cache. Around the engine sit several shells: maxengine_server.py wraps it in a gRPC model server, offline_engine.py builds a threaded worker pool around the same verbs for bulk jobs, and vllm_decode.py connects MaxText to vLLM so the sampler and scheduler come from there while JAX computes the forward pass. The CLI script inference/decode.py wires it all together for a single stream — encode the prompt, prefill, insert, generate in a loop, decode back to text, and assert the output matches autoregressive_decode_assert so the end-to-end path is testable.

The layer zoo underneath serving is shared with training: Embed, L60 covers the vocab table and logit head, while the RotaryEmbedding family at L231 implements RoPE and its Yaarn-style variants for different model families. Attention kernels are pluggable — the attention config selects among fused implementations, several of which trace back to the same ideas popularized by flash-attention — and quantization (AqtQuantization for weights/activations, separate kv-quant) is threaded through the projections. Converting HuggingFace checkpoints into Orbax format, documented in checkpoint_conversion/, closes the loop with transformers so you can train here and evaluate elsewhere.

From Install to Your First Model

MaxText is Linux-first and Python 3.12-first, and the docs now recommend uv throughout. From a fresh clone of the repository:

git clone https://github.com/google/maxtext.git
cd maxtext
uv venv --python 3.12 --seed maxtext-env
source maxtext-env/bin/activate

# from-source install (TPU flavor; use .[cuda12] for GPUs)
uv pip install -e .[tpu] --resolution=lowest
install_tpu_pre_train_extra_deps

# verify the environment
uv pip check
python3 -c "import maxtext"
python3 -m maxtext.trainers.pre_train.train --help

Two details matter. The --resolution=lowest flag is not decoration: it pins every dependency to the exact versions the team tested, which is the practical answer to the JAX/jaxlib version-matrix problem on accelerators. And the install_*_extra_deps entry points fetch the accelerator-specific extras (a --with-tf flag adds optional TensorFlow/TFDS and JetStream dependencies) that are deliberately kept out of the base wheel.

With the environment healthy, the smallest real run is a synthetic-data smoke test — no dataset, no checkpoint, ten steps:

python3 -m maxtext.trainers.pre_train.train \
  model_name=llama3-8b \
  run_name=my-first-run \
  base_output_directory=gs://YOUR-BUCKET/maxtext-outputs \
  dataset_type=synthetic \
  steps=10

On a GPU box you’d instead pass the GPU YAML as the leading positional config, e.g. src/maxtext/configs/models/gpu/llama3-8b.yml. If you just want to poke at the config layer from Python, this snippet uses only verified API surface:

from maxtext.configs import pyconfig

config = pyconfig.initialize([
    "prog",                       # argv[0] placeholder
    "model_name=llama3-8b",       # inferred model config
    "run_name=smoke",
    "steps=10",
])
print(config.base_emb_dim, config.steps)   # 4096 10

Finally, generate text from a (randomly initialized) model to exercise the serving path: python3 -m maxtext.inference.decode run_name=my-first-run base_output_directory=... per_device_batch_size=1. The output will be gibberish without a converted checkpoint via load_parameters_path, but it proves the whole prefill/insert/generate loop compiles and runs.

Honest Limits

The trade-offs are real and the maintainers don’t hide them. First, this is TPU-first software: the happy path, the benchmark numbers, and most of the docs assume Google Cloud infrastructure — GCS buckets for output, gcloud tooling for workloads. GPU support is genuine (the cuda12 extra, GPU configs, FSDP-style prefetch variants), but a “decoupled mode” environment variable dance exists precisely because GCP assumptions are baked in. Second, config sprawl is the tax for flexibility: with a Pydantic schema of well over a thousand fields, finding which five knobs control your throughput is an archaeology exercise, and the restructure that moved MaxText/ to src/maxtext/ means a lot of blog posts and Stack Overflow answers from 2024 and earlier point at ghosts. Third, the whole design presumes multi-host orchestration — XLA wants to see the full device mesh, so single-node experimentation with large models is awkward, and running real workloads means XPK, Cluster Toolkit, or Pathways-style setups rather than a bare torchrun. Fourth, dependency pinning cuts both ways: --resolution=lowest buys reproducibility at the price of staying off the bleeding edge, and mixing JAX/jaxlib versions from different extras can break your environment in ways that are easier to nuke-and-recreate than to debug. None of these are disqualifying — they are the honest cost of a codebase that treats “train a frontier model on a pod of TPUs” as the normal case. For everyone else, it remains one of the cleanest blueprints for reading how compiler-driven LLM training is actually organized.
entry.summary: A source tour of Google's MaxText: the pyconfig config system, logical-axis sharding, the NNX training step, Orbax checkpointing, and the MaxEngine decode loop.

entry.title: NVIDIA NeMo: A Source Tour of the Typed-Module Architecture Behind Speech and Multimodal LLMs

link.title: NVIDIA NeMo: A Source Tour of the Typed-Module Architecture Behind Speech and Multimodal LLMs

entry.content:
NVIDIA’s NeMo (Neural Modules) is one of those frameworks that quietly backs a large fraction of the open speech models you have heard of — Parakeet, FastConformer, Canary, Magpie — while also carrying NVIDIA’s newer speech-aware language models. Unlike a thin training loop or a serving-only project, NeMo is an opinionated framework: every network is assembled from typed, reusable modules, every model lives in a config-driven Lightning subclass, and every checkpoint can round-trip through a single .nemo file. If you have read our earlier tours of PyTorch or inference servers like Triton Inference Server, this post completes the picture by showing where a framework like NeMo sits between them: it consumes PyTorch idioms upstream and produces deployable artifacts downstream.

The premise of the design is deceptively simple. A “neural module” takes typed inputs and produces typed outputs, and a “model” is just a trainable composition of those modules plus a YAML configuration. Everything else — the model registry that resolves names like nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2 from NGC or Hugging Face Hub, the checkpoint connectors, the experiment management around a Lightning Trainer — is machinery bolted onto that core contract. Reading the source of the current main branch, the shape of the repository is crisp: nemo/core defines the contracts, nemo/collections ships the ASR, TTS, audio and SpeechLM2 model families, nemo/lightning glues NeMo callbacks into PyTorch Lightning, and nemo/utils holds the experiment and checkpoint plumbing. Notably, the LLM training collection that earlier releases shipped under nemo/collections/llm has been split out of this repository, so today’s NeMo proper is speech- and multimodal-first — an important mental-model correction for anyone returning after a year or two.

In this tour we walk that architecture from the inside out: the base classes that every model inherits, the type system that validates wiring, the collections that package real models, the checkpoint format, and the export paths that get a trained model onto a server. The two diagrams below are generated directly from the source tree.

Overview of NeMo on main: the core class contract (Model, ModelPT, NeuralType, SaveRestoreConnector, Exportable) anchors three consumer sides — the ASR and TTS collections, the SpeechLM2 collection with its shared tokenizers, and the Lightning/exp_manager wiring that turns configs into training runs.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Model, L983 — the abstract hub every NeMo model inherits: Typing, Serialization, FileIO and HuggingFaceFileIO mixins, plus the class-method from_pretrained registry at L1015.
  • ModelPT, L53 — the LightningModule base for classic NeMo models, with config-driven __init__, dataset and optimizer setup, and .nemo save/restore built in.
  • NeuralType, L32 — the semantic dtype-and-axes type system that checks ports between modules before you ever launch a run.
  • SaveRestoreConnector, L43 — the pluggable connector that packs model YAML, weights and artifacts into a single .nemo archive.
  • Exportable, L40 — the mixin that gives models declared input/output names and an export() entry point for deployment formats.
  • ASRModel, L34 — abstract speech-recognition base with an auxiliary-loss registry and CUDA-graph toggles, parented by EncDecCTCModelBPE, L40 and EncDecRNNTBPEModel, L39.
  • SALM, L57 — the Speech-Aware Language Model: a LightningModule + HF-hub mixin that interleaves audio embeddings with text tokens.
  • CallbackGroup, L25 — a singleton that fans NeMo lifecycle hooks out to registered callbacks.
  • exp_manager, L478 — the one-call setup function that wires loggers, checkpointing and resume logic around a Lightning Trainer.

Core Classes: the Model Contract

The whole framework hangs off four abstract classes in nemo/core/classes. Typing lets a module declare input_types and output_types as dictionaries of NeuralType objects — each carrying an element kind (spectrogram, embeddings, labels…) and axes kind (batch, time, channel…). When you connect a Conformer encoder to a decoder, NeMo compares these types and refuses to wire incompatible ports; the comparison logic lives in nemo/core/neural_types/comparison.py. This is the single most “NeMo” idea in the codebase: rather than trusting shapes alone, modules carry meaning about what a tensor is.

Serialization and FileIO define save_to/restore_from, and Model composes them. ModelPT then merges that contract with PyTorch Lightning: its constructor takes an OmegaConf cfg plus an optional Trainer, and __init_subclass__ enforces bookkeeping on every subclass. The data-facing methods — setup_training_data, L544, setup_validation_data, and setup_optimization, L628 — are driven entirely by sub-configs of the model YAML, so the same class trains on different datasets without code changes. Optimizer construction funnels through configure_optimizers, L859, which combines NeMo’s core/optim schedulers with standard PyTorch optimizers.

Below the model level sits NeuralModule, L70, a torch.nn.Module with Typing and Serialization mixed in. Encoders, decoders, augmentations and data-processing blocks all inherit from it. A good example is ConformerEncoder, L65, which declares typed audio input/output ports, supports streaming masks, and can be checkpointed or exported as a unit.

Collections: ASR, TTS, SpeechLM2

The nemo/collections tree is where users actually live. The ASR collection separates models (CTC, RNN-T, hybrid, diarization, classification) from parts (submodules like conformer blocks and decoding strategies) from modules (encoders and decoders). The hybrid family — EncDecHybridRNNTCTCModel, L38 — stacks an RNN-T decoder and a CTC decoder over one encoder, and its transcribe() method at L96 is the entry point most users meet first. Decoding is pluggable: greedy and beam strategies for both CTC and RNN-T live in asr/parts/submodules, including batched beam search with CUDA-graph acceleration.

The TTS collection is organized around two abstract bases: text-to-spectrogram models like FastPitchModel, L82, and vocoders like HifiGanModel, L45, both descending from the SpectrogramGenerator/Vocoder pair declared in base.py, L64. Text normalization and grapheme-to-phoneme conversion feed them from the g2p and torch subpackages. The shared tokenizer stack — SentencePieceTokenizer, L125 plus helpers like get_megatron_tokenizer, L187 — lives in nemo/collections/common/tokenizers and is reused by every collection.

The newest collection, speechlm2, reflects a different design point: models there are LightningModules paired with a Hugging Face-style hub mixin rather than ModelPT children. SALM, L57 combines a text LLM with an audio encoder via AudioPerceptionModule, L45, and DuplexS2SModel extends the pattern to full-duplex speech-to-speech. There is even a vLLM plugin model, NeMoSpeechLMForConditionalGeneration, L116, that registers SALM directly into the vLLM multimodal registry for serving.

The detailed view: inheritance inside the core (Model → ModelPT; NeuralModule → typed ports), the ASR/TTS/SpeechLM2 model families, the callback-and-checkpoint wiring, and the utils that hold save/restore and export helpers together.

Checkpoints, Artifacts, and the .nemo Format

NeMo’s portability story rests on one file format. ModelPT.save_to at L392 writes a .nemo archive — a tarball containing model_config.yaml, a Lightning checkpoint, and any registered artifacts — while restore_from, L434 unpacks it, rebuilds the model from its YAML, and loads weights. The actual packing is delegated to SaveRestoreConnector, L43, which is deliberately pluggable: sharded, model-parallel, or storage-backend-specific variants can subclass it.

Artifacts deserve special mention. Models can call register_artifact, L234 to bind an external file (a tokenizer model, a language-model for shallow fusion, a phoneme dictionary) into the checkpoint, so the archive is self-contained. During restore, class references inside the YAML are resolved by import_class_by_path at L566, with an allowlist of safe import prefixes guarding against arbitrary code execution from untrusted checkpoints — a security detail that a lot of serialization frameworks skip.

The registry side of the story is Model.from_pretrained: given a name with a / it resolves through Hugging Face Hub support in HuggingFaceFileIO, L26; otherwise it matches against each class’s list_available_models() entries and downloads from NGC into a cache directory. This dual-source registry is why the same from_pretrained call works for both stt_en_* NGC names and nvidia/* Hub names. Distributed users get extra machinery: AppState, L34 tracks model and data-parallel ranks so save_to refuses plain archives in model-parallel mode, and checkpoint file names get rank-injected to keep sharded saves consistent.

Training Wiring Around the Trainer

NeMo deliberately does not wrap the Lightning Trainer; it decorates it. exp_manager takes the trainer and an ExpManagerConfig, creates the log directory, configures loggers (TensorBoard, W&B, MLflow, DLLogger), installs checkpointing via NeMoModelCheckpoint, L39, and handles resume logic that can find the last checkpoint in a prior experiment. On the callback side, NeMo-specific hooks inherit BaseCallback, L19 and are aggregated by the CallbackGroup singleton, which ModelPT.__init__ pokes with on_model_init_start the moment a model begins construction. This split — Lightning owns the loop, NeMo owns domain hooks — is what lets the same model class train on one GPU or scale out behind a Megatron-style strategy without code changes.

A subtle but useful piece: ModelPT.maybe_init_from_pretrained_checkpoint at L1263 lets a fresh model initialize parts of itself (usually just the encoder) from a pretrained .nemo file as declared in its config — the standard transfer-learning path for ASR fine-tuning. Combined with exp_manager’s resume support, warm-starting is declarative rather than scripted.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation follows the standard PyPI path, with extras controlling the (heavy) dependency tree:

pip install nemo_toolkit[all]

Then transcription is three lines, using the exact registry path described above:

import nemo.collections.asr as nemo_asr

model = nemo_asr.models.ASRModel.from_pretrained(model_name="nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2")
model.transcribe(["meeting.wav"])

ASRModel.from_pretrained resolves the Parakeet hybrid RNN-T/CTC model, downloads the .nemo archive into the cache, unpacks it, rebuilds the model from its embedded YAML and loads weights — all through the Model/SaveRestoreConnector machinery we traced. For training rather than inference, you hand a Trainer to the constructor and let exp_manager set up the rest; the model’s YAML carries train_ds, validation_ds and optim sections that setup_training_data and setup_optimization consume. Saving a fine-tuned model back out is one call to save_to("my_parakeet.nemo"), and if you want to share it, the HuggingFaceFileIO mixin provides push_to_hf_hub for the Hub counterpart of the registry you downloaded from.

Export and Serving Paths

Deployment is a first-class concern rather than an afterthought. The Exportable mixin lets each model declare its export input/output names, supported formats and any disabled deployment ports; the base export() implementation at L61 drives conversion to ONNX and TorchScript, with the ExportFormat enum and verification helpers (numerical comparison against the eager model, ONNX Runtime session checks) in export_utils.py, L95. Module-swap utilities replace training-only kernels with export-friendly equivalents before tracing. The exported ONNX can then feed standard runtimes — our ONNX and ONNX Runtime tours cover that side of the fence.

Serving has two flavors in today’s tree. Classic NeMo served RNN-T/CTC models as RNNT/CTC services over gRPC, and NVIDIA’s historical FasterTransformer/TRT-LLM bridges carried NeMo checkpoints into high-throughput LLM servers — see our FasterTransformer and Triton Inference Server tours for that trajectory. The newer path is native: the SpeechLM2 collection ships its own vLLM plugin so a SALM checkpoint can be loaded by vLLM directly through the registered wrapper class, no manual conversion step. For Hugging Face-centric workflows, push_to_hf_hub plus transformers-compatible tokenizer exports round out the interop story.

Honest Limits

The dependency tree is the first thing to respect: nemo_toolkit[all] pulls Lightning, OmegaConf, Hydra, k2, lhotse, sentencepiece, text-normalization toolkits and more, and version drift between those pins has historically been the top source of install pain. The framework’s coupling to PyTorch Lightning is similarly double-edged — Lightning gives you distributed training and checkpointing for free, but debugging means reading Lightning’s callback order, and NeMo adds its own callback layer on top.

Second, the codebase has churned hard. The jump from NeMo 1.x to 2.x replaced the nemo/collections/nlp stack, and since then the LLM-training collection itself moved out of this repository — so older tutorials referencing nemo/collections/llm or nemo/collections/nlp paths will not match this tree. ModelPT-based speech collections keep the 1.x-style YAML-driven flow, while speechlm2 models use a newer HF-hub style; both idioms coexist, which is honest engineering mid-migration but confusing at first contact.

Third, assumptions skew GPU-centric. CUDA-graph decoding, TE/megatron-adjacent optimizers, and Sharded-model defaults all presume an NVIDIA stack; CPU-only inference works but is not the optimized path. Finally, the .nemo tarball format, while self-contained, embeds class-import paths in its YAML — restoring an archive across NeMo versions can fail when class paths move, so pin your version per checkpoint and keep restore_from’s strict=False in your back pocket for legacy files.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of NVIDIA NeMo: collections architecture, ModelPT and PyTorch Lightning training, the .nemo model registry and restore flow, NeuralType contracts, and export paths to ONNX and vLLM serving.

entry.title: open_clip: A Source Tour of the Maintained Open CLIP Implementation

link.title: open_clip: A Source Tour of the Maintained Open CLIP Implementation

entry.content:
When OpenAI released CLIP in 2021 it changed how the community thinks about vision-language pretraining: two towers, a temperature-scaled contrastive objective, and zero-shot classification from prompt templates. The original repository — which we walked through in the earlier tour of /clip/ — shipped the weights and a minimal inference API, but training was never its focus. Its code froze shortly after release, and anyone who wanted to retrain, fine-tune, or extend CLIP had to start over. That gap is exactly what mlfoundations/open_clip fills. Begun as a community reimplementation of the contrastive objective, it has grown into the de facto maintained implementation: hundreds of pretrained checkpoints, native support for the SigLIP, CoCa, CLAP and MaMMUT model families, timm and HuggingFace backbones behind one factory function, and a full training package that scales from a single GPU to a multi-node cluster.

The library is deliberately thin. It is pure Python on top of PyTorch — no compiled extensions, no Cython to build, nothing to fight with on Windows or ARM — and it leans on two ecosystem workhorses that most projects already trust: timm for vision backbones and transformers for text encoders, the same library behind /transformers/. That combination is the quiet design decision that makes open_clip feel bigger than it is. A ViT-B-32 config is a handful of JSON keys; a ConvNeXt or EVA vision tower is borrowed from timm at instantiation time; a multilingual XLM-R text tower is borrowed from transformers the same way. The library adds contrastive glue, checkpoint conversion, and a registry, not another modeling framework.

This post is a source tour, in the same style as our previous posts. We start at the function every user touches first — the model factory — then descend into the pretrained-weight registry, the tokenizer bridge, and the distributed training and zero-shot evaluation flow. Two dependency graphs drawn from the actual repository structure anchor the narrative: an overview of the whole system and a detail view of how the pieces call each other.

Overview of open_clip: the training entry wires the factory, the weight registry, the tokenizer bridge, the dual-tower models, and the train/eval flow into one call graph.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L62 — the CLI entry that parses arguments, initializes the distributed device, creates the model and data, and drives the epoch loop.
  • create_model_and_transforms, L1251 — the one-stop factory returning a model plus paired training and validation preprocess transforms.
  • _PRETRAINED, L460 — the curated weight registry mapping every model and tag to a checkpoint URL or HuggingFace repo.
  • CLIP, L412 — the canonical dual-tower model with encode_image / encode_text and a learnable logit_scale.
  • VisionTransformer, L550 — the native ViT image tower; the same file hosts the causal-masked text tower and attention blocks.
  • HFTokenizer, L625 — the HuggingFace AutoTokenizer bridge that adapts arbitrary tokenizers to CLIP conventions.
  • TimmModel, L25 — the adapter that turns any timm classification backbone into a vision tower.
  • train_one_epoch, L296 — the autocast step loop with gradient accumulation, loss reduction, and metric logging.
  • build_zero_shot_classifier, L22 — builds class embeddings from prompt templates for end-of-epoch evaluation.

The Factory: One Entry Point, Many Model Families

Everything in open_clip funnels through create_model_and_transforms in src/open_clip/factory.py. It delegates to create_model, L326, which first parses the model identifier. A bare name like ViT-B-32 is looked up in the built-in configs under src/open_clip/model_configs/ — roughly 150 JSON files, each describing embed_dim, vision_cfg, and text_cfg. A prefixed name like hf-hub:org/repo instead fetches an open_clip_config.json from the HuggingFace Hub, and local-dir: reads the same format from disk. Three input styles, one config schema.

Class selection is the interesting part. Rather than hard-coding class names, the factory calls traits_from_config, L144 to classify the config into a ModelFamily, then picks the implementation: plain CLIP for the classic flat layout, CustomTextCLIP (L613) when the text tower should stay a nested module — required for HF-backed, “modern”, or variable-length text towers — plus CoCa, CLAP, MaMMUT, and the generative NaFlex classes. Once instantiated, the model exposes the familiar encode_image, L488 and encode_text, L508 methods, both with an optional normalize flag.

Weight loading is its own sub-flow. load_checkpoint, L255 accepts .safetensors files through the safetensors reader and everything else through torch.load with weights_only=True by default. Before the state dict reaches the model it is massaged: third-party checkpoints are remapped by convert_state_dict, L278, legacy flat-layout checkpoints are re-keyed into the custom-text format, logit-scale shapes are reconciled, and vision or text position embeddings are interpolated if the checkpoint’s grid size differs from the requested one. This is where years of ecosystem drift get absorbed so that a 2021 OpenAI checkpoint and a 2026 community checkpoint both load through the same call.

The Pretrained-Weight Registry

The registry in src/open_clip/pretrained.py is what makes tags like openai, laion2b_s34b_b79k, or datacomp_xl_s13b_b90k mean anything. _PRETRAINED, L460 is a large dictionary keyed by architecture, where each value maps tags to config dicts built by helpers such as _pcfg for OpenAI-style defaults. Crucially, the config carries more than a URL: it records the normalization mean/std, the resize mode, the interpolation, and a quick_gelu flag, because the original OpenAI models were trained with the QuickGELU activation and silently degrade if you run them with vanilla GELU. When a tag’s activation setting disagrees with the requested architecture variant, the factory emits a QuickGELU mismatch warning rather than letting accuracy evaporate quietly.

Lookup and download are separated cleanly. get_pretrained_cfg, L806 answers “what are the settings for this tag”, while download_pretrained, L922 resolves the checkpoint to a cached file, preferring GitHub release URLs or HuggingFace Hub downloads (download_pretrained_from_hf at L885). Over the project’s life most weights have been mirrored from GitHub releases to timm/* and laion/* Hub repos, which matters because release assets lack CDN-grade bandwidth. Several newer checkpoints ship as safetensors — the format we covered in /safetensors/ — which the loader detects by file extension and reads without pickle deserialization. For pure inference there is a shortcut, create_model_from_pretrained, that fuses model creation and transform construction in one call.

Tokenizers: the HuggingFace Bridge

The original CLIP used a bespoke byte-pair encoder trained on its caption corpus. open_clip keeps that exact implementation as SimpleTokenizer, L264, complete with the bundled BPE vocabulary, so OpenAI checkpoints tokenize identically here and in the original library. Everything newer, though, rides on HFTokenizer, L625, a wrapper around AutoTokenizer — the same dispatch layer we described in /tokenizers/. The wrapper does three things that look small and are not: it forces right-side padding so CLIP’s eos-pooling math stays correct for decoder-family tokenizers that default to left padding, it maps bos/eos/cls/sep ids into the sot/eot vocabulary the towers expect, and it applies a configurable text-cleaning chain before encoding.

Selection happens in get_tokenizer, L850: the model’s text_cfg decides between the HF bridge, the SigLIP sentencepiece tokenizer (SigLipTokenizer, L896 with Gemma, C4, or multilingual variants), a tiktoken-based tokenizer for the generative models, or the original BPE. The same text_cfg also declares context_length — 77 for classic CLIP, much longer for SigLIP and modern variants — and the factory cross-checks pad and eos ids against the pooling mode so a generative model cannot silently train with the wrong ignore index. The lesson from reading this file is that “just tokenize it” hides most of the compatibility surface in multimodal systems.

From Install to Your First Model

The package installs from PyPI under its distribution name open_clip_torch:

pip install open_clip_torch
# training extras (webdataset, pandas, transformers):
pip install "open_clip_torch[training]"

Then the full factory round-trip in a few lines:

import torch
from PIL import Image
import open_clip

model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms(
    "ViT-B-32", pretrained="laion2b_s34b_b79k"
)
tokenizer = open_clip.get_tokenizer("ViT-B-32")

image = preprocess(Image.open("dog.jpg")).unsqueeze(0)
text = tokenizer(["a diagram", "a dog", "a cat"])

with torch.no_grad(), torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16):
    image_features = model.encode_image(image)
    text_features = model.encode_text(text)
    image_features /= image_features.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    text_features /= text_features.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    text_probs = (100.0 * image_features @ text_features.T).softmax(dim=-1)

print(text_probs)  # per-class probabilities

Note what you did not do: no manual config parsing, no weight conversion, no activation-function bookkeeping — the tag carried all of it. Every API used above (create_model_and_transforms, get_tokenizer, encode_image, encode_text, the laion2b_s34b_b79k tag) exists verbatim in the current source tree, and the returned preprocess object is built by image_transform_v2, L501 from torchvision primitives on the mean/std the registry recorded for that tag.

Training, Distributed by Default

The open_clip_train package is where “reproduction” stops being a claim and becomes a script. main, L62 enables tf32, calls init_distributed_device, L80 — which reads torchrun’s LOCAL_RANK/RANK/WORLD_SIZE environment variables or SLURM’s equivalents, initializes torch.distributed with nccl, gloo, or hccl, and pins the device to the local rank — then assembles data with get_data, L1203, the optimizer with create_optimizer, L336 (weight-decay exclusions for norms, biases, and the logit scale, plus optional layer-wise decay), and the schedule with cosine_lr, L74. Precision is centralized in get_autocast, L6: one flag selects amp fp16, pure fp16, bf16, or fp32, and the loop picks the matching input dtype and gradient scaler.

The step loop in train_one_epoch is honest engineering rather than magic. Each batch flows through the task object — the TrainingTask contract (L30) with CLIPTask (L9) as the contrastive implementation — whose forward returns a dict of losses computed by ClipLoss, L57, a symmetric cross-entropy over the scaled image-text similarity matrix. The SigLIP objective swaps it for the pairwise sigmoid SigLipLoss, L375, and distillation and CoCa variants subclass the same base. Because open_clip is pure PyTorch underneath, every collective here is a plain dist.all_reduce — the native code path we touched on in /pytorch/ — so nothing exotic hides inside the C extensions; there are none. An --local-loss option slices the contrastive matrix per rank to save memory, and evaluation runs after each epoch through the zero-shot classifiers built from OPENAI_IMAGENET_TEMPLATES, L2, the same 80 prompts the original paper used.

Detail view: CLI and IO, the factory and its weight plumbing, the model families, tokenizer and preprocess builders, the task abstraction, the training loop, and the zero-shot eval chain.

Honest Limits

No tour is complete without the trade-offs. First, pretrained-weight licensing varies dramatically across the registry: the OpenAI originals, LAION-2B, DataComp, SigLIP, and MetaCLIP checkpoints come with different licenses and different dataset provenance, and open_clip deliberately does not normalize that away — you are expected to check the tag’s source repo before deploying. Second, checkpoint size management is on you. Registry entries now span 150 MB RN50s to multi-gigabyte ViT-bigG and EVA models; the library caches whatever you download, offers no deduplication or sharding, and load_checkpoint will happily keep both the flat and custom-text copies of a state dict in memory during conversion. Plan disk and RAM accordingly.

Third, training-data dependence is structural. CLIP-family models inherit the curation, biases, and coverage of their caption corpora — a DataComp-tuned ViT-B-32 and a LAION-tuned one of the same architecture are not interchangeable, and zero-shot gaps on underrepresented classes trace directly to what the contrastive objective saw. Fourth, tokenizer differences matter more than users expect: the original CLIP BPE, HF tokenizers, sentencepiece SigLIP variants, and tiktoken-based generative tokenizers are not drop-in swappable, text embeddings are not portable across checkpoints with different vocabularies, and the classic 77-token context length is an architectural constraint, not a soft default. Finally, quickGELU and preprocessing mismatches are silent until you evaluate — the warnings exist, but only comparison against published numbers will catch a subtle preprocessing drift. Treat the registry’s mean/std/interpolation fields as part of the model definition, because that is how the source treats them.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of mlfoundations/open_clip: the model factory, the pretrained-weight registry, the HuggingFace tokenizer bridge, and the distributed training flow with zero-shot evaluation.

entry.title: Optimum: How HuggingFace Routes Transformers Models to Every Accelerator

link.title: Optimum: How HuggingFace Routes Transformers Models to Every Accelerator

entry.content:
If you have ever typed pip install optimum[onnxruntime] and watched a PyTorch checkpoint turn into an ONNX Runtime model with one class swap, you have met Optimum at its best. Optimum is HuggingFace’s optimization toolbox that sits beside Transformers as an extension of Transformers, Diffusers, timm and Sentence-Transformers, and its job is simple to state and hard to do well: take the same model you already loaded and run it faster on whatever hardware you actually own, whether that is a CPU, a GPU, an Intel NPU, an AWS Inferentia chip or a Habana Gaudi. Under the hood it is a large family of exporters, quantizers and optimized model wrappers — the ONNX Runtime ones being the oldest and best documented, which is why the ORTModelForXXX classes remain the reference point for the whole design.

The repository has quietly reinvented itself in the last couple of years. What used to be one giant package holding every exporter has been carved into optimum-* sibling distributions — optimum-onnx, optimum-onnxruntime, optimum-intel, optimum-neuron, optimum-habana and more — while the core optimum package keeps the shared contracts: the task router, the exporter configuration base classes, the optimized model base class, the quantizer interface, a full GPTQ implementation and a torch.fx toolkit. The CLI discovers installed backends at runtime through Python namespace packages, which is why the same optimum-cli binary grows subcommands as you install extras. This tour reads the core at commit 0df84f2 on main, mapping how a model travels from from_pretrained to a hardware-specific artifact.

The Optimum core: the CLI dispatches through subpackage discovery into the task router, export contract, model base and quantization stack.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L188 — the optimum-cli entry point; it registers root subcommands, calls load_subpackages(), then parses argv and runs whatever service was bound to the chosen subcommand.
  • ExportCommand, L20 — the export subcommand, a thin shell that hands model-plus-task resolution to each backend’s exporter CLI.
  • load_subpackages, L72 — scans installed distributions whose names start with optimum- and boots their subpackage modules so backends can register their own CLI commands.
  • TasksManager, L118 — the routing brain: task-name-to-model-class mappings for transformers, diffusers, timm and sentence-transformers, plus inference of task, library and framework.
  • get_exporter_config_constructor, L1236 — resolves which exporter config class applies to a given model type and task combination.
  • ExporterConfig, L77 — the base contract every backend config inherits: a normalized config class, dummy input generator classes and the absolute tolerance used to validate converted outputs.
  • OptimizedModel, L93 — the base class of ORTModelForXXX, OVModelForXXX and friends, with from_pretrained(export=True) doing on-the-fly conversion.
  • OptimumQuantizer, L10 — the two-method quantizer contract (from_pretrained + quantize) that ORTQuantizer, OVQuantizer and the GPTQ quantizer all implement.
  • Transformation, L85 — the reversible torch.fx rewrite primitive behind graph optimization and tensor parallelism.

One Core, Many Accelerators

The most consequential file in the repo is also one of the smallest. optimum/subpackages.py defines load_namespace_modules (L30), which iterates over installed distributions, filters for names starting with optimum-, explicitly skips optimum-quanto and optimum-nvidia to keep CLI startup fast, and imports each distribution’s subpackage module. That module, in turn, registers backend commands onto the CLI. In other words, Optimum’s plugin system is just Python packaging: there is no registry file to edit, no entry_points ceremony — install optimum-neuron and optimum-cli grows Inferentia capabilities.

This is also why the installation table in the README is the real user interface of the project. pip install "optimum[onnx]" gets you pure ONNX export; optimum[onnxruntime] adds the inference wrappers; optimum[openvino], optimum[neuronx], optimum[habana], optimum[amd] and optimum[furiosa] each pull a different hardware stack with its own GitHub repository and docs. The core repo deliberately holds none of that code. When you read a tutorial that imports from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForSequenceClassification, that import resolves through the optimum namespace into the optimum-onnxruntime distribution — the class exists, but it does not live in this repository anymore. ExecuTorch support follows the same pattern through optimum-executorch, PyTorch’s native on-device runtime for mobile and edge (our ExecuTorch tour covers that runtime itself).

The payoff of the thin-core design is that shared behavior only gets written once. Config loading, weight saving, tokenizer persistence and task inference are core concerns; hardware-specific graph surgery is not.

From Install to Your First Model

Install the ONNX Runtime extra (the --upgrade-strategy eager flag matters because the subpackages pin tightly against each other):

python -m pip install --upgrade --upgrade-strategy eager optimum[onnxruntime]

The fastest path is the CLI, which exercises ExportCommand and the TasksManager for you:

optimum-cli export onnx --model gpt2 gpt2_onnx/

Programmatically, the canonical flow — straight from the repo’s own quickstart documentation — swaps one import. Setting export=True tells from_pretrained to trace the PyTorch checkpoint to ONNX during loading:

from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForSequenceClassification
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

model_checkpoint = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
save_directory = "tmp/onnx/"

# Load from the Hub and export to ONNX in one call
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_checkpoint)
ort_model = ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_checkpoint, export=True)

# Persist the ONNX graph and the tokenizer together
ort_model.save_pretrained(save_directory)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(save_directory)

That save_pretrained call is inherited from OptimizedModel (modeling_base.py, L118) and reuses the shared save utilities that persist tokenizers next to optimized weights. Quantization is a second, symmetric step — build a quantization config, wrap the exported model in a quantizer, call quantize:

from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTQuantizer
from optimum.onnxruntime.configuration import AutoQuantizationConfig

qconfig = AutoQuantizationConfig.arm64(is_static=False, per_channel=False)
quantizer = ORTQuantizer.from_pretrained(ort_model)
quantizer.quantize(save_dir=save_directory, quantization_config=qconfig)

The result is a model_quantized.onnx file you can reload with the same ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(save_directory, file_name="model_quantized.onnx") call and run with a plain forward pass — no framework lock-in, since the weights are ONNX tensors on disk and the runtime is just ONNX Runtime.

The Routing Brain: TasksManager

Everything above depends on one deceptively hard question: given a model id, what is it for? TasksManager (L118) answers it with a stack of class-level mapping tables — _TRANSFORMERS_TASKS_TO_MODEL_LOADERS, _DIFFUSERS_TASKS_TO_MODEL_LOADERS, _TIMM_TASKS_TO_MODEL_LOADERS — that tie task tags like text-classification or automatic-speech-recognition to auto-model class names. The mappings tolerate ambiguity: where one task maps to several candidate loaders (for example speech models that can be AutoModelForSpeechSeq2Seq or AutoModelForCTC), the value is a tuple and the auto-class’s internal _model_mapping picks the right one.

Inference flows through three cooperating methods. infer_task_from_model (L800) reads the model config’s task hints, falling back to Hub metadata and eventually to head-inspection heuristics. infer_library_from_model (L958) decides whether the object belongs to transformers, diffusers, timm or sentence-transformers. Then get_model_from_task (L1083) instantiates the right auto-class, and determine_framework (L582) settles the PyTorch-versus-TensorFlow question with a version- and availability-aware policy. Extension is a first-class citizen: create_register (L290) returns a decorator that backend packages use to register their config classes per model type and task, and get_all_tasks (L1063) plus synonyms_for_task (L420) normalize the task vocabulary so text-classification and friends resolve consistently.

The same file also normalizes config chaos. Different architectures name the same concept differently — one model’s num_attention_heads is another’s d_model — and standardize_model_attributes (L1004) papers over those differences before export. The per-architecture config wrappers themselves live in NormalizedConfigManager (optimum/utils/normalized_config.py, L209), which exporters consult to find the right attribute names for inputs, outputs and dynamic axes.

Quantization: the Contract and the Flagship

The quantization surface starts from a deliberately tiny abstract base. OptimumQuantizer (quantization_base.py, L10) declares from_pretrained and an abstract quantize (L23) and nothing else. Every backend quantizer — ORTQuantizer for ONNX Runtime, OVQuantizer with NNCF for OpenVINO — shapes itself to that two-call contract, which keeps user code portable across hardware.

One quantizer is still implemented in the core repository: GPTQ. GPTQQuantizer (optimum/gptq/quantizer.py, L64) is a complete post-training quantization flow for PyTorch modules. Its quantize_model method (L334) runs the layer-wise GPTQ algorithm against a calibration set, select_quant_linear (L199) picks the best available quantized-linear kernel for your hardware, and after quantization post_init_model (L607) and pack_model (L627) wire in the packed kernels and optionally compile the result. Calibration corpora are built in gptq/data.py — prepare_dataset (L34) assembles wikitext2, C4 or PTB samples — and evaluate_perplexity (optimum/gptq/eval.py, L7) gives you a quick degradation check before you ship. The layer-discovery helper get_layers (optimum/gptq/utils.py, L33) finds the nn.Linear-family modules worth quantizing, including transformers’ quirky Conv1D layout.

torch.fx: Rewrites and Tensor Parallelism

The third pillar is a torch.fx toolkit that predates much of PyTorch’s own parallelism tooling. On the optimization side, Transformation (L85) defines a lint-and-recompile wrapper with signatures and per-node bookkeeping, and ReversibleTransformation (L176) adds undo. Concrete rewrites include MergeLinears (L237), which fuses adjacent linear layers sharing an input into one bigger GEMM, and FuseBiasInLinear (L393), which folds bias adds into the matmul. These are the graph-level tricks exporters and runtime benchmarks both benefit from.

On the parallelism side, parallelize_model (optimum/fx/parallelization/api.py, L46) takes a model plus a device mesh and produces a sharded module. A shared ParallelExecutionCtx (core.py, L107) carries world size and process groups through the pass framework (PassBase, passes.py, L45), where ParallelAxisSolverPass (L144) decides which tensor dimension each op should shard along. DecompositionInterpreter (decomp.py, L78) breaks composite ops into aten primitives so the per-op handlers in the Registry (op_handlers.py, L25) can map them onto sharded replacements like ColumnParallelLinear (linear.py, L33) and VocabParallelEmbedding (embedding.py, L25), with collectives such as all_reduce (dist_ops.py, L22) implemented as differentiable autograd functions.

Honest Limits

The subpackage split is the right call and it still hurts. Nine accelerator extras in the install table means nine dependency matrices to keep coherent, and the README’s insistence on --upgrade-strategy eager is a confession that version skew between optimum, optimum-onnx and optimum-onnxruntime is a recurring failure mode. Documentation has largely caught up, but search engines have not: many blog posts and Stack Overflow answers still import classes from optimum.onnxruntime paths that now resolve through a sibling distribution you may not have installed.

Deprecation churn is real, too. The codebase is mid-rename: ExportConfig is a deprecated alias that warns on subclassing and points to ExporterConfig (optimum/exporters/base.py, L68); from_pretrained warns that encoding the revision as model@revision will be removed in v1.23 (optimum/modeling_base.py, L331). Pin versions or read the changelog before upgrading.

Export fidelity has inherent ceilings. Tracing works on real tensors, so control flow that depends on tensor values gets frozen, and configs gate on MIN_TORCH_VERSION via is_torch_support_available (L211) because some operators only export cleanly on newer toolchains. Post-export validation compares outputs within an absolute tolerance and raises typed errors like AtolError when numerically sensitive models drift — a safety net, not a fix. And while GPTQ quantization in the core is solid, the wider quantization story is deliberately fragmented across backends, so a quantized model built for one runtime is not guaranteed to load in another.

Finally, maintainership is spread thin by design. Optimum competes for the same “serve this model fast” niche as serving-first stacks like TGI and vLLM, and the honest answer is that Optimum is the conversion-and-optimization layer you reach for when you own the deployment target yourself.

Where Optimum Fits

Optimum is best understood as the bridge between the HuggingFace modeling ecosystem and the hardware below it. Above, it accepts anything Transformers can load; below, it emits artifacts for runtimes from ONNX Runtime through OpenVINO to edge runtimes, and it quantizes along the way. If your deployment story starts with “a model checkpoint from the Hub” and ends with “a specific chip,” the path runs through this repo’s contracts — the task router, the exporter config, the optimized model base — even when the code doing the heavy lifting lives in a sibling optimum-* package.
